title: Twelve steps
hook: Alcoholics Anonymous blends honesty, surrender and service, with a "higher power" each person defines

segments.voice: Yesterday, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy: seeing a harsh thought as an event in the mind. Your line was thoughts aren't facts. Did the words I'm having the thought that loosen anything? Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

A church basement on a weeknight. Folding chairs in a circle, a coffee urn hissing in the corner, a plate of cookies nobody has touched yet. Someone stands, says their first name, and then a sentence that may have taken years to say out loud. The room answers with their name, warmly, all together. Nobody asks what they do for a living. Nobody asks which church, if any, they belong to. The church only lends the room. On the wall there may be a poster, a numbered list. It's a spiritual path that grew up outside any one religion, in rooms like this one. Today, the twelve steps.
screen: `FOLDING CHAIRS, A COFFEE URN.` → `A FIRST NAME, A HARD SENTENCE.` → `A NUMBERED LIST ON THE WALL.`

segments.voice: The twelve steps come from Alcoholics Anonymous, whose founders are known in the fellowship as Bill W. and Dr. Bob. In plain paraphrase, the path runs like this. It begins not with strength but with an admission: I'm powerless over alcohol, and my life has become unmanageable. Then: I've come to believe a power greater than myself could restore me to sanity. Then a decision to turn my will and my life over to the care of God, as each person understands God. That phrase is the hinge. The steps don't say which God. Some members mean the God of their childhood faith. Some mean nature, or love. Some, by their own account, mean the group itself, the circle of chairs. The middle steps are honesty, made concrete: a searching moral inventory, written down, then admitted to God, to yourself, and to one other human being. Then a list of everyone you've harmed, and amends wherever they won't cause more harm. The last step is service: carrying the message to someone still struggling. Surrender, honesty, repair, service. And holding it all up is a saying you'll hear in those rooms: one day at a time. Not forever. Just today. The saying has an older cousin in the Gospels: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself." Neither line says tomorrow doesn't matter. Both say it can't be carried today. AA's own tradition says the only requirement for joining is a desire to stop drinking. If drinking or drugs are a struggle for you, that door is open, and other fellowships adapt the same steps.
screen: `STEP ONE: AN ADMISSION, NOT STRENGTH.` · `GOD, AS EACH PERSON UNDERSTANDS GOD.` · `INVENTORY, AMENDS, SERVICE.` · `ONE DAY AT A TIME.` · then, large: `TAKE THEREFORE NO THOUGHT FOR THE MORROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think what you'd surrender. Settle, and breathe. Ask quietly: what am I trying to control on my own that isn't working? A habit. A person. A worry I keep gripping. Let one thing come forward. Now picture holding it in your hands, and then setting it down, in front of whatever you trust: God, if you pray; the people who love you; life itself. You're not giving up on it. You're giving up carrying it alone. Stay with the open hands. The bell holds the time.
Twelve steps. The path of Alcoholics Anonymous: admit powerlessness, turn to a power greater than yourself, take an honest inventory, make amends, and carry the message on. Today's word.
Your line: one day at a time. Today, when the thing you set down tries to climb back into your hands, ask only: can I leave it down until tonight? Just today. Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

howItsDone: People in Alcoholics Anonymous and other twelve-step fellowships attend meetings, work through the steps with a sponsor who has walked them before, and practice service by helping newcomers, taking recovery one day at a time.

myth: AA requires members to believe in one particular God
it speaks of God as each person understands God. some members mean the group itself.
the steps begin with an admission of powerlessness
not with strength: I'm powerless, and my life has become unmanageable.
the last step is about keeping your recovery private
it's service: carrying the message to someone still struggling.

fork.setup: you've tried for years to stop drinking by willpower alone, and it keeps failing. what does step one ask?
options: admit you're powerless over it and your life has become unmanageable.
wait until you feel strong enough.
fork.reveal: the twelve steps start with defeat, honestly admitted. in AA's telling, that admission is where change begins.

trapdoor: what you thought: the twelve steps are rules for quitting drinking.
what it means: a spiritual path of surrender, honesty, repair and service, lived one day at a time.
what a scholar hears: a path born outside any one religion that leaves God open, as each member understands God.

sources.ref: The Twelve Steps, in Alcoholics Anonymous (the 'Big Book'), chapter 5
The Twelve Traditions, Tradition Three (the only requirement for membership)

sources.quoted: Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself.

notes: All AA text is paraphrased; no AA wording is quoted (the Big Book's copyright status was not checked). Steps 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8–9 and 12 are paraphrased; confirm 'God, as each person understands God' fairly renders 'God as we understood Him'.
The index hook's date (1939) is left out under the claims rule; founders named only as 'Bill W. and Dr. Bob', without dates or places.
'Some, by their own account, mean the group itself' reflects AA literature's acknowledgment that some members take the group as their higher power; confirm.
'One day at a time' is described as a saying heard in the rooms, not attributed to a specific AA text.
Matthew 6:34 is offered as an older parallel without ranking; confirm the framing is welcome on this path.
Help line: the script points listeners to AA (the only requirement is a desire to stop drinking) and says other fellowships use the same steps. Confirm the wording is accurate and not promotional.

Editor pass: 'AA never says which God' (an absolute claim) became 'the steps don't say which God'; cut 'free' from the help line (not in the cited Tradition Three) and 'use the same steps' became 'adapt the same steps'; the fork reveal now frames the admission as AA's telling rather than the narrator's claim. Matthew 6:34 KJV wording checked.
